concepts.partName: The Hyderabad State and Its Financial Crisis
concepts.bodyMd:
The Hyderabad state was founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk Asafjahi in **1724**, and his descendants continued to rule it until **1948**. Under Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911–1948), the Nizam Government surrendered following the Police Action of the Indian Government, and the state was merged into the Indian Union on **17th September 1948**.

Throughout the long period of Nizam rule, the administration was run by Diwans (Prime Ministers) assisted by ministers and other officials. **Siraj-ul-Mulk** served as prime minister to Nizam **Nazir-ud-Doula (1829–1857)**. When Siraj-ul-Mulk died in 1853, **Salarjung** was appointed Prime Minister in his place, with the British intervening to secure his appointment.

**Financial and administrative distress before Salarjung:** Repeated territorial and financial losses steadily weakened the state, plunging it into a severe financial crisis by 1853.

*   In 1766, the Northern Sarkars (coastal districts) were taken over by the British.
*   In 1800, further ceded districts were taken by the British.
*   In 1853, the Nizam surrendered three rich districts — **Berar, Raichur, and Darashiv** — to the British under the Treaty of Berar.
*   The state suffered financial exploitation through the Palmer and Company dealings, and through Chouth and Sardeshmukhi tax collection imposed by the Marathas.
*   The Nizam state was also drawn into Maratha and Mysore wars under British pressure.
*   With no proper administrative machinery to manage these pressures, the state and the Nizam were forced to mortgage their lands at high interest merely to meet day-to-day administrative expenses.

concepts.partName: Salarjung's Early Life and Rise to Power
concepts.bodyMd:
Salarjung's original name was **Mir Turab Ali Khan**; "Salarjung" (1829–1883) was his popular title. Before becoming Prime Minister, he served as Talukdar (Collector) of Medak District in Telangana.

*   He became Prime Minister (Diwan) of Hyderabad State on **31st May 1853**, following the death of his uncle Siraj-ul-Mulk, at the young age of **24**. He was a western-educated young man, appointed with British support.
*   He continued as Diwan until his death in **1883**, serving under three rulers in succession: **Nasir-ud-Doula (1829–1857)**, **Afzal-ud-Doula (1857–1869)**, and **Mir Mahaboob Ali Khan (1869–1911)**.
*   When the sixth Nizam, Mir Mahaboob Ali Khan, ascended the throne in 1869 as a **three-year-old minor**, Salarjung gained the opportunity to effectively and independently establish his authority over the administration of the state.

**Why the British backed Salarjung's measures:**

1.  During the **1857 revolt**, Salarjung and the Nizam sided with the British and helped suppress the uprising in the state.
2.  The modernization of Hyderabad ultimately served colonial interests, so the British supported his reform program.

Salarjung directed his first attention toward resolving the financial crisis of the state, and from there proceeded to comprehensive administrative reform.

By Salarjung's time, the Hyderabad State covered **82,698 sq. miles**, with a population, per the 1881 census, of **98,45,594**. The kingdom was a union of three regions: **Marathwada, Telangana, and Karnataka**. For administrative convenience, it was organized into subhas (provinces), sarkars (districts), and mahals (sub-districts).

Administrative reform proceeded in two stages: skillfully formulating measures, and implementing them with ability — Salarjung succeeded in both.

### Provinces (Subhas)

Under the first Nizam, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asafjah, the state had **six subhas**: Aurangabad, Berar, Bijapur, Bidar, Hyderabad, and Khandesh. Due to later political developments and treaties with the British, all except Khandesh remained under Nizam control by Salarjung's time.

### Divisions (1867)

In 1867, Salarjung divided the Hyderabad State into **five divisions**:

| Division | Headquarters |
|---|---|
| North Western | Aurangabad |
| Western | Bidar |
| Southern | Gulbarga |
| North | Patancheruvu |
| East | Bhuvanagiri |

Each division was headed by a **Sadar Talukdar**, equivalent to a Revenue Commissioner in British India. The Sadar Talukdar held all revenue, civil, and criminal powers within the division, and also supervised the district officers (Talukdars/Collectors) below him. He was assisted by two officers — one for revenue matters, one for judicial matters — both paid officials who executed the instructions of the concerned ministry. Each division comprised three to four districts.

### Districts

Prior to Salarjung, districts were controlled by tax farmers or contractors. In **1855**, he replaced this system by appointing **paid Talukdars (Collectors)** over district administration, and in **1865** introduced the **"Zilabandi"** system.

Under Zilabandi, the state was divided into **fourteen districts**:

| No. | District |
|---|---|
| 1 | Aurangabad |
| 2 | Parbhani |
| 3 | Nanded |
| 4 | Indur (Nizamabad) |
| 5 | Bhir |
| 6 | Bidar |
| 7 | Medak (Methuku Seema) |
| 8 | Elagandula (Karimnagar) |
| 9 | Naldurg |
| 10 | Sholapur |
| 11 | East Raichur |
| 12 | West Raichur |
| 13 | Warangal (Khammam was then part of Warangal) |
| 14 | Nalgonda |

By **1880**, two more districts — **Nagarkurnool** and **Gulbarga** — were created, based on total revenue, bringing the count to sixteen. Districts were graded into three categories by annual revenue:

| Category | Annual Revenue |
|---|---|
| First | More than Rs. 12,00,000 |
| Second | Up to Rs. 10,00,000 |
| Third | Up to Rs. 8,00,000 |

Each district was headed by a Talukdar or Collector, assisted by other officials. Talukdars themselves were divided into three categories, each with three internal grades and a distinct salary scale:

| Talukdar Category | 1st Grade | 2nd Grade | 3rd Grade |
|---|---|---|---|
| First category | Rs. 1,000/month | Rs. 800/month | Rs. 600/month |
| Second category | Rs. 450/month | Rs. 400/month | Rs. 300/month |
| Third category | Rs. 300/month | Rs. 250/month | Rs. 200/month |

The first Talukdar (Collector) headed the district with subordinate staff and was responsible for revenue income and expenditure, collection of revenue, export and import taxes, and resolving some civil and criminal disputes. He was assisted by Deputy Talukdars, clerks (Gumasthas), Judicial Officials, Revenue Officials, and Treasury Officials; district records were maintained with the help of "Amla" clerks or departmental clerks.

### District Reorganization (1868)

A further round of district reorganization took place in **1868**, modeled on the **Bombay pattern** rather than the Madras pattern followed elsewhere. Revenue administration posts of **Avval, Duyyam, and Suyyam Talukdar** were created (Talukdar being equivalent to Collector), with a **Board of Revenue** established to supervise the Collectors. For administrative convenience, the state was divided into **five divisions, sixteen districts, and 114 taluks**:

| Division | Districts | Taluks |
|---|---|---|
| North | Medak, Indur (Nizamabad), Elgandal (Karimnagar) | 23 |
| East | Khammam, Warangal, Nalgonda, Nagarkurnool | 26 |
| West | Bidar, Nanded, Naldurg | 25 |
| South | Raichur, Sholapur, Gulbarga | 14 |
| Northwest | Aurangabad, Parbhani | 26 |

### Taluks

Salarjung further divided districts into **Taluks**. At the start of his period there were **74 taluks** in the Diwani region; by 1880–81 this had risen to **107**. The distribution by district included: Aurangabad-8, Bhir-7, Parbhani-6, Bidar-5, Nanded-8, Naldurg-7, Raichur-5, Lingasagoor-4, Sholapur-4, Gulbarga-6, Indur-9, Medak-5, Elagandula-7, Khammam-9, Nalgonda-5, Nagarkurnool-8, Sirpur Tandur-3, and Altaf Balda-1.

Taluks were headed by **Tahasildars**, graded into three levels by salary:

| Grade | Monthly Salary |
|---|---|
| First | Rs. 150 |
| Second | Rs. 125 |
| Third | Rs. 100 |

Tahasildars administered revenue, judiciary, police, and other matters within the taluk, assisted by subordinate paid clerks (Gumasthas), revenue officials, and judicial officials.

### Cities

After the taluk, the next administrative unit was the city, headed by a **Kotwal** — the Chief Officer of the city responsible for police, peace, and order. Separate officials handled city revenue, income and expenditure, and judicial and other city matters.

### Villages

The village was the last administrative unit. Salarjung introduced several reforms in village administration, involving the following functionaries:

*   **Patwaris** — kept land records of the village and assisted in collecting land revenue from villagers, paid on a **2 paise commission** basis.
*   **Revenue Patels** — assisted the Patwari in land revenue collection, also on a **2 paise commission** basis.
*   **Police Patel and Talari** — looked after law and order in the village, paid a commission of **2 paise** from tax collected in the villages.
*   **Dade** — assisted visiting state officials and worked as a postman, paid a **4 paise commission** from the local fund.
*   **Nirukadu** — looked after water storage and release to fields from the tanks.
*   **Sethusindu** — each protected fifty houses in the village and assisted the Police Patel in maintaining peace and order.

All of these village functionaries drew their income from the **"Grama Seva Funds."**

### Central Administration

The overall administration of the state was carried on under the control of the Prime Minister or Diwan, who was also called Regent. He was assisted by the Deputy Prime Minister, the British Resident, the Finance Minister, and Heads of Departments/Branches, who gave suggestions and advice. The British Resident's role was advisory, limited to political and economic issues.

*   By **1880–81**, the administration had **14 departments**: Judiciary, Revenue, Police, Public Works, Education, Health, Municipal Corporation, Army, Finance, Postal, Railway and Telegraph, Nizam Sarf-i-Khas land department, Political affairs, and Judicial & Legislative Acts department.
*   These fourteen departments were broadly grouped under **seven departmental ministers** — Judiciary, Revenue, Police, Public Works, Education, Health, and Municipal Corporation — each titled **"Sadar-ul-Miham."** They were assisted by Secretaries and subordinate staff, and were ultimately responsible to the Prime Minister, who in turn — along with his bureaucracy — was responsible to the king. The king could accept or reject ministerial advice; supreme authority in the kingdom rested with him.
*   In **1868**, administration was brought under **four departmental ministers**, called **"Sadar-ul-Mahams":**

| Department | Minister |
|---|---|
| Revenue | Nawab Mukaram-ud-Doula Bahadur |
| Judiciary, Jails | Bhasheer-ud-Doula |
| Police | Shamsher Jung Bahadur |
| Public Works, Education & Health | Shahebjung Bahadur |

Alongside these ministers, the Deputy Prime Minister, "Ashja-ud-Daula" Munirjung Bahadur, gave key suggestions and advice on administrative issues; his advice was always accepted by the Prime Minister, who would discuss it with the Nizam before decisions were taken. Ultimately, the Nizam himself was the highest authority — his orders were law, his court the highest judicial court, and he was Commander-in-Chief of the army. He could accept or reject any advice given to him.

Salarjung established the judicial institution most effectively and gave the judiciary **autonomy**, with separate **civil and criminal** jurisdictions. An independent judicial branch, separate from executive administration, already existed in the state from **1846**; Salarjung built on this foundation and strengthened it considerably, establishing **Sessions Courts** at district headquarters and organizing the High Court at Hyderabad with a Chief Judge and four judges to hear Diwani (civil) and Fauzdari (criminal) appeals.

### Judicial Institutions Before Salarjung's Later Reforms

After becoming Prime Minister, Salarjung initially established judiciary of three types:

1.  **Adalat-e-Padushahi**, formed in 1853.
2.  A judicial institution to decide disputes between the Nizam's soldiers and Sikh soldiers, established in 1855.
3.  A new judicial institution established by an official named **Govind Rao** in 1860, to decide civil disputes in the Ilaka Peshkar areas.

### Later Reforms Under Diwan Salarjung

*   He established the **Sadar-ul-Miham Adalat** in **1869** for judicial matters in the Diwani region.
*   The first Law Minister appointed in the Nizam kingdom was **Nawab Basheer-ud-Daula Bahadur**, assisted by a secretary and Gumasthas (clerks). 

*   The Law Minister handled civil and criminal cases in the city and Muffasil regions, and issued orders to protect law and justice. If a judgment was found erroneous and no justice had been done, it was mandatory to take the Prime Minister's permission to re-enquire and decide the case.

*   In **1872**, Diwan Salarjung made key changes to the judiciary by establishing the **Court of Appeal**, named **"Mahakama-e-Murafa-e-Ajla."** It had a Presiding Officer and four members, and was described as the "Appellate Court of Judicature." 

*   It decided all types of civil and criminal appeal cases from the city and districts, made rules and regulations for the smooth functioning of the various courts, and was the final authority in all judicial matters after the Diwan.

*   In civil judicial administration, **"Majlis-Aliya Adalat"** (the **High Court**) was the key judicial court. A person punished in a lower court could file a petition in the High Court. Its powers and structure:
    *   It decided civil disputes in Hyderabad city and cases involving monetary value.
    *   Below it were Divisional courts, District courts, Taluka courts, City courts, and courts to decide religious disputes; there were also separate courts for border disputes.
    *   It had powers to reduce or cancel severe punishments, including death sentences.
    *   It could impose life sentence and **39 rope beats**.

### Punishment Powers by Judicial Level

| Level | Officer | Imprisonment | Fine & Rope Beats |
|---|---|---|---|
| Division | Sadar Talukdar | 10 years | Rs. 4,000; 39 rope beats |
| District (1st) | First Talukdar | 4 years | Rs. 1,000; 39 rope beats |
| District (2nd) | Second Talukdar | 2 years | Rs. 500; 15 rope beats |
| District (3rd) | Third Talukdar | 1 year | Rs. 300; 15 rope beats |
| Taluk | Tahasildar | 6 months | Rs. 150; 12 rope beats |
| City | Kotwal/Police Commissioner | 3 years | Rs. 500; 39 rope beats |
| Village | Police Patel | 4 days | Rs. 3; — |

### Court Statistics During Salarjung's Period

There were **five divisional courts, seventeen district courts** under the first Talukdar/Collector, **22 courts** under the second Talukdar, **19 courts** under the third Talukdar, and **103 courts** under Tahasildars. There was one city court under the Kotwal/City Police Commissioner and one High Court at the capital, Hyderabad. 

In the Diwani area of Hyderabad State, there were **168 criminal courts**, and among civil courts there was a separate Arabs Court, a Kazi Court, and a city border court to deal with disputes not settled elsewhere; there were also 6 courts for disputes with other cities in the kingdom. The **total civil courts** in the Diwani area came to **172**.

### Judicial Salaries

| Post | Monthly Salary |
|---|---|
| Chief Judge, High Court | Rs. 1,200 |
| Other Judges, High Court | Rs. 600 |
| Border court judges (city border disputes) | Rs. 2,400 |
| Kazi Court Chief | Rs. 500 |

Notably, border court judges were paid more than the Chief Justice of the High Court. Judges were appointed purely on merit, and only moral and honest people could secure appointments.

Salarjung separated the **police department from the revenue department**, a key structural reform.

### Structure

*   An **Amin (Inspector)** was appointed for every two Taluks, with an **Additional Inspector** for a large Taluka. Each part was assisted by an Attached Police Official.
*   The kingdom was organized into **five parts**, each headed by a **Naib Sadar Muhatamin**, titled **Deputy Inspector General of Police**.
*   Each district had a **Superintendent of Police (Muhatamin)**, responsible for supervising the district's entire police force and controlling the Inspector of each Taluka.
*   Police Constables were appointed for each district, along with police personnel known as **"Sovers."**
*   Both Superintendents and Inspectors of Police had assistants called Gumasthas.
*   There were **three classes each** of Superintendents of Police and Inspectors of Police.

Appointments in the police force were made purely on merit and moral character.

### Salaries by Grade

| Post | 1st Grade | 2nd Grade | 3rd Grade |
|---|---|---|---|
| Superintendent of Police (District Head) | Rs. 200/month | Rs. 170/month | Rs. 140/month |
| Inspector (Taluka Police Head) | Rs. 110/month | Rs. 100/month | Rs. 90/month |

In **1869**, the police force was reorganized, and a separate **police secretary** was appointed to oversee the entire police administration, brought under ministerial control. The first police minister was **Nawab Shamsher Jung Bahadur**.

### Force Divisions and Strength

The police force was divided into two divisions: the **General Police Force** and the **Village Police Force**.

*   General Police Force constables earned Rs. 7 or 8/month and could be promoted up to Head Constable based on performance; Inspectors were also promoted on performance.
*   By **1879–90**, the General Police Force strength stood at **14,055**, of which **3,250** were allotted to city duties and **10,805** to district duties. At the Taluk level, **"Out Posts"** were established under a Head Constable or Jamedar.
*   At the village level, law and order was entrusted to the **Police Patel**, assisted by the Talari and Sethusindus — each Sethusindu protecting fifty houses.
*   City police administration was led by the **Kotwal (City Police Commissioner)**, with subordinate staff and a force protecting the lives of the people.

Overall, the police hierarchy ran: **Deputy Inspector General** (division) → **Superintendent of Police** (district) → **Amin/Inspector** (taluka) → **Police Patel and Sethusindu** (village).

Salarjung reorganized the military of the Nizam Kingdom.

*   In **1864**, he built a dedicated building for supervising the Nizam's army, staffed by a Secretary and an Assistant. The Secretary of the Military Branch handled expenditure, appointments, transfers, and issue of ordinary military orders, and specially reviewed the permanent battalions.
*   **Kalandhar-Bardhars** (officials) submitted representations and appointments of temporary soldiers to the Diwan.
*   In **1875**, the government established the **"Daftar-e-Najam Jamiyat"** (the Military Office).
*   In **1869**, the **Mansaf Office** was established.
*   In **1876**, a **Military Secretary** was appointed, responsible for military appointments and reviews, as well as other issues concerning temporary soldiers; the **Mansabdar offices** were established under his supervision.
*   Military personnel were trained under European officials, with overall supervision by the British.

Despite these efforts, Salarjung's attempts to fully modernize the armed forces — including plans to introduce machinery in state workshops — did not succeed; the Hyderabad army remained un-modernized on modern lines despite his best efforts.

Salarjung's main intention was to give the state economic stability, and revenue reform was the most important strand of his overall reform program.

### Land Classification

The entire state land was divided into **four parts**, each carrying different tax levies:

| Land Type | Share of Total Area | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Khalsa (Diwani) | 60% | Under direct government control |
| Sarfekhas | 10% | Expenses of the Nizam Nawab's daily maintenance |
| Paigah lands | (combined 30% with Jagirs) | Maintenance of Paigah military nobles |
| Jagirs | (combined 30% with Paigah) | Granted to various people on different merit |

In the Sarfekhas, Paigah, and Jagir areas, different land revenue collection systems prevailed and there was no direct administrative control by the Diwani government.

### Abolition of the Tax Farming System

Corrupt land revenue collection through tax farming — under which daftardars paid a fixed amount to the state while collecting more from peasants — exploited both peasants and the state, and kept peasants out of direct contact with the state. Recognizing this defect, Salarjung, after assuming office, abolished the tax farming system and removed the tax farmers (daftardars).

*   He appointed paid **Talukdars (Collectors)** in place of the daftardars, bringing peasants into direct contact with the state, relieving them of daftardar exploitation, and enabling Salarjung to know the exact income of the state.
*   The basis of revenue collection was shifted from the **village to the individual**, with differential rates based on land quality — eliminating middleman exploitation while increasing government revenue.

### The Sarbarasta System and the Rise of Landlordism

Even before Ryotwari was extended across the state, revenue collection in Khalsa (government) villages was carried out through a **middleman auction system**. Under this arrangement, known as **"Tahutta"** or **"Sarbarasta"** (also called **"Bilmakta"**), the right to collect a fixed amount of tax from a locality for a set period was auctioned off, and the strongest bidders in each area — typically the locally powerful — secured these rights. Once the auction term ended, the right could change hands again. 

During the Sarbarasta period, the contractors (tahutdars/bilmaktadars) were required to pay the government only the fixed contracted amount, while collecting far more from the peasants for themselves — building up substantial wealth in the process. Salarjung abolished this system, surveyed and settled land holdings directly, and introduced the practice of the government's own machinery collecting revenue straight from the peasant. 

Until then, prominent contractors under the Sarbarasta system had been granted titles such as **Deshmukh, Deshpandya, Deshai,** and **Sardeshai**, along with compensation payments (parihars) when the system was withdrawn.

*   These titleholders — the Deshmukhs, Deshpandyas, Deshais, and Sardeshais — had, over the years, registered vast tracts of land in their own names and become large landlords, particularly in the Khammam, Nalgonda, Mahbubnagar, and Warangal districts, where landlords holding over 500 acres each controlled **60 to 70 percent** of the land.
*   A survey conducted in **1942** found **3,668** such Deshmukhs, Deshpandyas, Deshais, and Sardeshais across the state.
*   This concentration of land in the hands of a landlord class, rooted in the old revenue-farming system, later became a central grievance behind the Telangana peasant movement.

### Revenue Board (1864)

Salarjung established the **Revenue Board** in **1864** to supervise the revenue administration institution in the Diwani regions and areas taken over from the British. It had a President and four members, and Mukkaram-ud-Daula signed the orders issued by the Board, which supervised revenue administration under the Diwan's control. 

In **1875**, the British Government at the Centre established an **Inam Office**, headed by an Inam Commissioner, which took possession of unnecessary and misused Inam lands and merged them with the Khalsa/Diwani lands.

### Zilabandi System (1865)

Salarjung introduced **"Zilabandi"** in **1865** to streamline revenue administration, alongside the **Jamabandi** system of annual land recording.

*   The state was divided into **fourteen Zillas (Districts)**, each headed by an **Avval Talukdar (District Collector)**, assisted by **Doyam Talukdars (Sub-Collectors)** — all paid officers responsible for revenue collection and law and order.
*   Districts were divided into Taluks administered by paid Tahsildars and their subordinate staff, responsible for revenue, law, and order.
*   The fourteen districts were grouped into **five regional divisions**, each headed by a Sadar Talukdar — equivalent to a Revenue Commissioner of British India — responsible for revenue and other matters across the division and lower levels.
*   At village level, Patwaris handled revenue collection with Patels assisting them, both paid on **commission, not salary**, and working on a **hereditary basis**, meaning a successor would take over the position after the incumbent — intended to build good local understanding over the long run.

### The Ijara (Lease) System

To resettle villages that had become depopulated, Salarjung introduced another arrangement alongside Ryotwari, known as the **Ijara (lease) system**, aimed at bringing suitable land back into cultivation. Under this scheme, land was leased out at a nominal rent in the initial stage; the rent was then increased gradually and systematically, and eventually the full assessed rate was collected. The Ijara system was itself withdrawn in **1908**.

### Ryotwari Settlement (1857)

Salarjung introduced the **Ryotwari system** in the state in **1857**. The settlement period under this system was initially fixed at **20 years**, and later reduced to **15 years**; each new settlement carried an opportunity to raise the assessed tax.

*   In line with this settlement policy, **wet (tari/magani) cultivation** was made compulsory in suitable areas.
*   Pattadars who had, at their own expense, developed dry land into wet land — for instance by digging wells — were nonetheless assessed at the higher wet-land (tari) rate on such land.
*   Wet land was assessed at **Rs. 20–25 per acre**, against **Rs. 10–12 per acre** for dry land — a heavier tax that remained in force until it was abolished after the formation of Andhra Pradesh.

### Survey and Settlement

The **"Survey and Settlement Department"** was established to survey lands, fix boundaries, and decide land type, headed by a special Commissioner. A Superintendent of Revenue Surveys was appointed, assisted by Deputy Superintendents; there were four or five such Superintendents across the Nizam kingdom.

*   The survey was first successfully conducted at **Aurangabad**, and afterwards, in **1877**, at **Naldurg**.
*   The **Ryotwari system** of land revenue was adopted, and **patta rights** were granted to individual ryots.
*   The annual recording of lands was called **"Zamabandi,"** carried forward from this point.
*   Land measurement used a **10-yard chain**; a **"Biga"** — equivalent to **6/6 chains, or 3,600 square yards** — was the unit of land, still in use as a unit in Telangana.
*   Ryots were permitted to pay land tax in either cash or cereals, which the government could store in warehouses.

These revenue measures together led to an increase in land revenue of around **Rs. 2,09,21,971 by 1880–81**.

### Overall Revenue Growth

The increase in land revenue and customs revenue placed the state's fiscal system on a sound footing.

*   Total public revenue was around **Rs. 0.8 million in 1853**, rising to about **Rs. 35.0 million by 1883**.
*   This increase was accompanied by a **reduction in public expenditure**, achieved by abolishing the private military troops of Rohillas and Pathans and their salaries, and by reducing irregular troops, allowances, assignments, and mansabs.
*   Increased revenue combined with reduced expenditure enabled the government to reduce its enormous public debt to a minimal amount — public debt fell from around **Rs. 35.0 million in 1848** to **Rs. 4.1 million by 1882**.
*   This drastic debt reduction, in turn, enabled the government to abolish **tankahi mahalat Jagirs** and the system of contracting or farming in Diwani areas.
*   The improved fiscal position was accompanied by the establishment of a **central treasury**, replacement of private bankers with **state treasuries** in districts and taluks, and introduction of a formal **budget system** with a special **Accountant General** and subordinate staff for maintaining income and expenditure accounts.
*   **Private mints owned and financed by Jagirdars were abolished**, and a state monopoly on minting was established, introducing a **uniform system of coinage** based on the **"Halisicca" rupee**.

When Salarjung became Diwan, there was no dedicated Revenue Institution or Administrative Institution in the Nizam kingdom. The Nizam had mortgaged valuable lands and jewellery and taken loans for government maintenance, and was due to pay **Rs. 50,00,000** to the British for loans taken. The resource-rich Raichur, Darashivam, and Berar regions had been taken under British control.

### Recovery of Mortgaged Lands and Territory

*   After 1853, Salarjung was able to increase the area of Diwani land under his administration.
*   The Nizam gave the British the following, under the 1853 Agreement:

| Region | Income |
|---|---|
| Berar valley | Rs. 30,60,309 |
| Balghat | Rs. 5,48,601 |
| Western districts | Rs. 2,29,588 |
| Raichur district | Rs. 1,51,342 |

*   Before 1861, Diwani land covered **40,000 square miles**, but this later rose to **71,598 square miles** due to the cancellation of mortgages on lands, for which Salarjung was responsible.

### Role in the 1857 Revolt and British Rewards

*   Nizam and Salarjung assisted the British during the **1857 Indian Sepoy Revolt**: they controlled the attack on the Hyderabad Residency and imprisoned the rebels **Turrebaz Khan** and **Moulvi Allauddin**.
*   The British praised the Nizam Government's role in controlling the mutiny as unforgettable, and as reward, waived the loan of **Rs. 50,00,000** due from the Nizam.
*   The **Raichur** district, Ahmednagar, Darashivam, and Naldurg were returned to the Nizam in **1861**.
*   Separately, when **Raja Venkatappaiah Naik** of Sholapur revolted during the 1857 mutiny, Salarjung and the Nizam had him arrested (the Wanaparthi ruler Raja Rameshwar Rao arrested Naik and sent him to the Nizam, who surrendered him to the British); as a result, the British rewarded the Nizam with Sholapur territory.
*   Inam lands worth **Rs. 8,37,205** and Jagirs worth **Rs. 8,86,875** were surveyed and taken into government possession, further improving the kingdom's economy.

### Customs and Other Taxes

*   In **1860**, Salarjung prohibited and abolished taxes on imports and exports, while the Customs Department was given power to impose tax on **salt**; a taxation policy on goods was introduced.
*   **Highway taxes**, nominal before his tenure, were increased and collected more effectively.
*   A district-wise "cordon" (bandi) excise system was set up, auctioning off the rights to collect duty on toddy, opium (moha/afim), bhang, and ganja separately in each district, and a stamp duty was imposed on sale and purchase transactions.
*   In **1871**, coal was discovered in the **Singareni** region, prompting British efforts to introduce transport facilities to the coal mines.
*   In **1867**, a separate **forest department** was created under a Superintendent of Forest, bringing the state's forest resources under government control.
*   In **1861**, the stamp paper office was brought under the control of **Munshikhana**, and the sale of stamp paper became a government monopoly.

### Currency Reform and "Currency Profit"

At the time, government employees' salaries were paid by weight in the old **"Sugur Sicca"** coin. Salarjung had these converted and paid out instead in the new **"Hali Sicca"** coinage; the margin gained through this conversion — around **10 percent** — was credited to the state treasury and came to be known as **"Currency Profit."** 

This currency profit, together with peshkush payments from zamindars, local fund cess, stamp duties, and other fees, became one of the state's principal channels for increasing government revenue.

These financial measures together achieved fiscal stability and allowed Salarjung to carry forward his broader administrative reform program.

Effective administration required educated persons and trained technical staff, motivating Salarjung's educational reforms.

*   In **1855**, he established the first western educational institution, the **Darul Ulum School**, in Hyderabad city, teaching in Urdu, Persian, and English mediums.
*   The **City High School** (1870) and **Chadarghat High School** (1872) were established subsequently; in these, alongside oriental language subjects, **English was made a compulsory subject**.
*   A **School of Civil Engineering** was established in 1870 to produce technical staff for the Public Works Department — a unique government experiment. This school's location later became the site of **Hyderabad College**, which came to be known as **Nizam College** from **1887**.
*   **Madarasa-e-Aliya** was established in 1873 for the children of Salarjung and the nobility.
*   **Madarasa-e-Aizza** was opened in 1878 for children of the royal family.
*   The Nizam also donated funds for the establishment of the Aligarh Educational Institution — the present **Aligarh Muslim University** — with Hyderabad officials **Vicar-ul-Mulk** and **Mohsin-ul-Mulk** contributing to its improvement.
*   A separate **education department** was created in **1869**, tasked with establishing government schools in Hyderabad city and almost all districts. During Salarjung's administration, **162 schools** were established across the kingdom, comprising **105 Persian schools, 34 Maharastrian schools, 4 English medium schools, and 19 Telugu medium schools**.

Improved fiscal and budgetary conditions, the product of Salarjung's revenue and financial reforms, enabled him to launch transportation and public works programs.

### Railways

*   A railway line between **Hyderabad and Sholapur** was built in **1868**.
*   An agreement was made in **1870** between the British India Government and the Hyderabad State Government for a line between Wadi and Hyderabad, on the Madras–Bombay railway route.
*   Following the discovery of high-quality coal at **Singareni** in 1871, and rising demand for coal driven by railway expansion, the line was further extended to the coal-mine region via **Dornakal and Ellandu**, and on to **Vijayawada**.
*   Coal mines were also found in the north of the Nizam kingdom, at **Chanda** (present-day Maharashtra), and it was decided — and approved during Salarjung's tenure — to extend the railway there. The **Railway Company** collected three lakh pounds as capital.
*   The construction of this line was kept secret from the public, and a rumour spread in the kingdom that it would be unprofitable and lead to irreparable loss.
*   The first line, between **Secunderabad and Wadi**, opened to traffic in **1874**, but its returns remained low, as the line primarily served **British strategic interest** rather than the Hyderabad economy.
*   Hyderabad's efforts to independently raise capital in London money markets were strongly resisted by the colonial Indian government. The state eventually convinced the Home Office instead, and with help from the **National Provincial Bank of England**, floated the **"His Highness The Nizam's Guaranteed State Railway Company Limited."**
*   The lines to the coal fields and cotton-producing districts materialized only more than a decade after Salarjung's death.
*   During this period, initial surveys and negotiations were also undertaken with the colonial government to begin coal mining, and eventually in **1887**, the **Hyderabad (Deccan) Mining Company** — with two-thirds of its capital from the state government — began operations.

### The Chanda Railway Scheme Controversy

*   In **1880**, an intellectual group formed in Hyderabad State to discuss the state's problems. They formed a committee to examine the Chanda Railway Scheme when it was about to be implemented, headed by the Principal of Hyderabad College, **Dr. Agoranath Chatopadhya**, with **Mulla Abdul Qayyum** as a member.
*   The committee wanted to bring the full details of the railway scheme to public knowledge, but its request to the Nizam Government for scheme details was rejected, being treated as a threat to the government.
*   As a result, Agoranath Chatopadhya was removed from his job and, on **20th May 1883**, banned from the Nizam kingdom; the government also gradually suppressed the members opposing the Chanda Railway Scheme.
*   The scheme was nonetheless executed, and the **Bombay–Madras Railway Route**, via Gulbarga and Wadi in the Nizam kingdom, was started by the British; the Hyderabad railway route was completed in **1878**, connecting Hyderabad via Wadi to Bombay and improving transport facilities.

### Postal, Telegraph, and Roads

*   During **1856–57**, the **Telegraph Institution** was established, connecting Hyderabad to Bombay via Kurnool.
*   In **1862**, the **Postal Department** was established; from **1871**, the Postal Institution spread regular postal connections to all districts, talukas, and cities, functioning under a Post Master General. **Nawab Shah Sawar Jung** was appointed the first Post Master General of Hyderabad, and the first series of stamps were introduced.
*   **Telephone services** connected several districts starting in **1885**.
*   Roads between different districts were improved, along with construction of bridges and culverts, undertaken by the **Public Works Department (PWD)**. In **1868**, the Hyderabad–Sholapur road was laid, and further road works were pursued vigorously thereafter, including repair and maintenance of irrigation works.

**Broader significance:** Hyderabad became the first native state to finance and eventually own its own road and rail transport, coal mines, and later power generation. 

The infrastructural development and improvement of trade mechanisms — together with the restructuring of feudal social relations, especially the shift in revenue basis from village to individual — paved the way for **commercialization of the agrarian economy**, seen in the growth of cotton in Marathwada and, later, oil seeds in Telangana. Thus, Salarjung's reforms under his Prime Ministership laid the basis for **industrialization in Hyderabad**.

To improve administrative standards, Salarjung established the **Public Service Commission** during his tenure and recruited talented people from across the country.

*   **Mohammedia and Kayastha youth from Northern India** were selected in large numbers as employees of the Hyderabad State — including Syed Hussaini, Syed Bilgrami, Mahib Hussain, Syed Mehdi Ali, and Mohin-ul-Mulk — who became able administrators after joining service.
*   **Aghoranath Chatopadhyay**, a Bengali educationist and father of **Sarojini Naidu**, joined the Education Institution in the Nizam kingdom and later became Principal of Hyderabad College (present-day Nizam College).
*   **Ramachandra Reddy** and **Barrister Rudra** also joined service in the kingdom.
*   **Mirza Asha Baig**, grandson of the famous Urdu poet **Mirza Ghalib**, was invited to Hyderabad to educate Prince Mahaboob Ali Khan.
*   Salarjung introduced an **automatic promotion system** based on talent and hard work for government employees.

The recruitment of talented outsiders into state administration, over time, brought a new element into Hyderabad's social structure — the **"non-mulkis"** — emerging as a powerful social category. This led to conflict between **mulkis and non-mulkis**, which influenced state policy in various ways in later years and **laid the foundation for the Telangana Movement**. 

At that stage, the Nizam took measures to suppress mulki agitation against the non-mulkis. Through these reforms, Salarjung became the guiding figure of modern Hyderabad's administrative history.

### Personality and Legacy of Salarjung

Salarjung himself was a leading Jagirdar, belonging to a **Shia family** that had originally migrated from **Bijapur, Deccan**. His growing control over the state apparatus became a source of tension with the **Sunni aristocracy**, especially the **Paigah nobles**, whose maneuvers constrained several of his initiatives. 

After the death of the co-regent in 1877, he bitterly opposed the appointment of Paigah nobles to the post, but ultimately had to yield to British pressure. There was also serious tension between him and the traditional bureaucracy, particularly the daftardars (contract Talukdars) whom he replaced with paid Talukdars.

**The changing standing of the Diwan:** Up to the time of the sixth Nizam, Prime Ministers had held a much greater role in state administration than Salarjung eventually enjoyed. Earlier Diwans had drawn correspondingly large salaries tied directly to state income — **Arastu Jah**, who served as Diwan from 1777 to 1802, took one-eighth of the state's income as his salary; **Mir Jumla** received Rs. 22 lakh; **Munirul Mulk** received Rs. 6 lakh; and **Chandu Lal** drew one-sixteenth of state income. 

When state revenue began to shrink continuously, British Resident-General **Fraser** advised the Nizam that Diwans could not go on drawing salaries at the old scale and would need to reduce their own pay — a recommendation that led **Salarjung to cut his own salary to Rs. 14,000**.

**Relations with the Nizams:**

*   He served directly under two Nizams — **Asafjah IV and Asafjah V** — and his relationship with both was marked by contradictions.
*   In his early years, every major initiative he took was met with suspicion from the ruler, who perceived him as a British agent. Even at the height of his authority, whenever Salarjung attended the Nizam's court, he would humbly announce his own entry — "prevesapettu" — behaving like an ordinary servant seeking permission to enter, a telling sign of the ambiguity in his position despite his real power over the administration.
*   On at least **three occasions — 1859, 1860, and 1867** — he was on the verge of losing his position, and a fourth time faced deportation, but the British intervened in his favor each time:
    *   In 1860, British Resident **Colonel Davidson** intervened to let him continue as Diwan.
    *   The same occurred in 1867, with British Resident **Yule** intervening.
*   With the death of Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daula** in 1869, his three-year-old son **Mahbub Ali Khan** became ruler, and the British appointed **Salarjung and Kabir Bahadur** as co-regents to the young Nizam — giving Salarjung sufficient time to implement reforms successfully and act as **de facto ruler** of the kingdom.
*   During the rule of his father-in-law Siraj-ul-Mulk, Berar had been given to the British, creating distrust among the people toward the Salarjung family. Salarjung worked intensely to regain public trust, and — because of his loyalty to the British during the 1857 revolt — all regions **except Berar, Raichur, Darashivam, Osmanabad, and Sholapur** were returned to the Nizam, partly removing the earlier distrust.

**Relations with the British:**

*   His relationship with the British was also marked by extremes: he was honoured with the title of **Knight Commander of the Star of India (KCSI)** by the Queen, yet on one occasion was threatened with deportation to the Madras Presidency.
*   The relationship was governed by the shifting unity or conflict of interest between the colonial rulers and the native government: his support to the British during the 1857 disturbances pleased them, and his later infrastructural measures received colonial support when they suited British interests — but on issues where the British perceived a threat to their power, he was opposed by the Residents. 

*   Notable contentious issues included the restoration of cotton-surplus Berar to Hyderabad (Berar remained with the British) and his unsuccessful attempts to modernize the armed forces.

*   In all, during his thirty years as Prime Minister, he was threatened four times with dismissal by the Nizams, including once with deportation. He submitted his resignation four times but always withdrew it. He survived **two assassination attempts**.

**Death and assessment:**

*   He died suddenly on **8th February 1883**, at the age of **53**, officially ascribed to cholera.
*   He was trained under an English teacher, **"Dieton,"** whose guidance provided a base for his personality and his ability to work continuously under hard circumstances.
*   When he took up the Prime Ministership in 1853, the state was in a fall of chaos and corruption; under these circumstances, he brought economic and administrative stability to the state on all fronts, paving the way for industrialization in Hyderabad.
*   The **University of Oxford** honoured him with the title **"Doctor of Civil Law."**
*   Historian **Abdul Waheed Khan** described Salarjung as "one of the best statesmen of 19th century Hyderabad," while **William Diggbe** held that his reform measures led to the "renaissance of Modern Hyderabad."

Salarjung got the loan due from the Nizam to the British waived, secured the return of regions taken by the British, and expanded the extent of the kingdom. He took possession of the Diwani lands, cancelled debts on mortgaged lands, removed the Jagirdars from tax collection, and introduced new tax policy in the Diwani region. 

He introduced the **Ryotwari** and **Zilabandi** policies in 1865, established the **Board of Revenue**, and appointed Ministers of Revenue, Police, and Law. He established the **High Court** and reformed the judicial institution, appointed talented youth to key government posts, and brought reform to the Transport, Railways, Postal, and Telegraph departments — transforming the Nizam kingdom into a modern state, and making his role in nineteenth-century India a unique one, poised between tradition and modernity.
